items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: Vic Dickinson was the master of that and I played next to him for eight of the ten years we were at Condon’s.

ctx.x: I think by the time you get, if you’ve played as long as I have you know whether your chops are in good shape for instance on the given night, you know whether that band is swinging. If that band is swinging and your chops are in pretty good shape, I’ll try anything really, and I’m not worried about making a mistake. I’ve got enough confidence that what’s the worst that’s going to happen? I’m going to get fired? My reputation is going to go down the tubes because of one mistake or something? I’m not worried about…

aging, maturity, call it what you want. I choose my notes but it’s a matter of choice. I don’t think I — I listened to myself when I thought I was great, playing very intense stuff, and I haven’t liked it as much as I thought I did when I was playing it. You know what I mean? So I’m a firm believer in simplicity. Vic Dickinson was the master of that and I played next to him for eight of the ten years we were at Condon’s. Just a master of simplicity. And he had marvelous technique, but he would just lay it out…
When players in the 60s came along — Coltrane, Miles Davis — the music seemed to get, some of it, pretty angry. Was it something you listened to? Did it have an effect on you?
